note: Only rules confirmed on an official government page. Research notes: MILECHECKAPP/docs/rest-area-overnight-rules-2026-10-15.md

states.name: Alaska
states.answer: Yes, up to the time limit posted at that rest stop.
states.cars: Alaska sets no number of hours in its rules. You may not park or camp longer than the limit posted at the site.
states.camping: Camping is limited by the same posted limit.

states.name: Arizona
states.answer: ADOT sets no time limit, but camping is prohibited.
states.cars: No time limit stated by ADOT.
states.camping: Camping and campfires are prohibited at rest areas.

states.name: Florida
states.answer: Only briefly. Cars can stay 3 hours. Commercial drivers can stay 10 hours.
states.cars: 3 hours.
states.trucks: 10 hours for commercial drivers under federal hours-of-service rules.
states.camping: Camping is prohibited.

states.name: Hawaii
states.answer: Not overnight. Hawaii bans using a vehicle as a place to live or sleep on public property between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m.
states.cars: No one may use a vehicle for human habitation while parked on a road, highway or other public property from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.
states.camping: Parks, camps and recreation areas used under their own rules are exempt.

states.name: Idaho
states.answer: Yes, for up to 10 hours at interstate rest areas and 16 hours on other state highways.
states.cars: 10 consecutive hours at rest areas on interstates. 16 consecutive hours at rest areas on other state highways.
states.camping: Camping is prohibited.

states.name: Illinois
states.answer: Only briefly. A stop at an interstate rest area can't exceed 3 hours.
states.cars: 3 hours per stop at interstate rest areas. IDOT can post a shorter limit.
states.trucks: Same 3-hour limit. One marked space per vehicle.
states.camping: Camping and putting up tents or shelters are prohibited.

states.name: Kentucky
states.answer: Only briefly. Stays are limited to 4 hours in any 24 hours.
states.cars: 4 hours in any 24-hour period at rest areas on limited-access highways. The Transportation Cabinet can allow longer stays for safety.
states.trucks: Same 4-hour limit. Trailers can't be dropped or used as a relay point.
states.camping: The rule doesn't address camping.

states.name: Maryland
states.answer: No. Overnight parking is prohibited and visits are limited to 3 hours.
states.cars: 3 hours without a permit from the caretaker or State Police.
states.camping: Camping and overnight parking are prohibited.

states.name: Minnesota
states.answer: Cars can stop for up to 4 hours where posted. Commercial drivers can stay up to 10 hours.
states.cars: Up to 4 hours where posted, per MnDOT.
states.trucks: Up to 10 hours in a row to meet federal hours-of-service rules, in stalls built for commercial vehicles.
states.camping: Not addressed in MnDOT's policy.
states.source: Minn. Stat. 160.2721 and MnDOT rest area policy

states.name: Montana
states.answer: Yes. Overnight parking is allowed for up to 12 hours, in one space.
states.cars: Up to 12 hours, one parking space per vehicle, per MDT.
states.camping: Camping at Montana rest areas is prohibited.
states.source: MDT rest area page and MCA 60-6-202

states.name: Nebraska
states.answer: No overnight. Stays are limited to 10 hours and overnight parking is prohibited.
states.cars: 10 hours at most.
states.camping: Overnight camping and overnight parking are prohibited.
states.source: NDOT Rest Area Rules and Regulations

states.name: Nevada
states.answer: Yes, within a limit of 18 hours in any 2-week period.
states.cars: Parking, camping or occupancy is limited to 18 hours in any 2-week period. That's a total, not a per-visit limit.
states.camping: Counted under the same 18-hour limit.

states.name: New Hampshire
states.answer: New Hampshire sets no rest area time limit. Tents and sleeping on the ground are banned.
states.cars: No statewide time limit found.
states.camping: Pitching a tent, setting up a camping device or sleeping on the ground on public right-of-way or public property is prohibited without permission. The law doesn't address sleeping in a vehicle.

states.name: North Carolina
states.answer: No. NCDOT says staying overnight at its rest areas is prohibited.
states.cars: No overnight stays, per NCDOT.
states.camping: Camping is prohibited, and so are tents, booths and other structures.
states.source: NCDOT rest area list and 19A NCAC 02E .0407

states.name: Ohio
states.answer: You can rest in your vehicle, but don't leave it unattended for 3 hours or more.
states.cars: A vehicle left unattended for three hours without State Highway Patrol permission can be towed. The rule sets no limit for an attended vehicle.
states.camping: Camping is prohibited.

states.name: Oregon
states.answer: Yes, up to 12 hours in any 24-hour period.
states.cars: 12 hours within any 24-hour period.
states.camping: Setting up a tent or other structure, camping, or staying over 12 hours is prohibited.

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.answer: Only briefly. Stays are limited to 2 hours in a 24-hour period unless posted.
states.cars: 2 hours in a single 24-hour period, or the posted limit. A vehicle left 24 hours is treated as abandoned.
states.trucks: At rest areas off the interstates, commercial vehicle parking is prohibited unless posted.
states.camping: Overnight camping and tents are prohibited. Sleeping is only allowed inside a legally parked vehicle.

states.name: South Dakota
states.answer: Only to rest. Cars can rest up to 3 hours. Commercial drivers up to 10 hours.
states.cars: Resting in a vehicle for up to three consecutive hours.
states.trucks: Up to 10 consecutive hours for commercial drivers under federal hours-of-service rules.
states.camping: Camping at interstate rest areas is prohibited, and South Dakota's definition of camping includes staying in a vehicle.

states.name: Tennessee
states.answer: No. Overnight parking isn't allowed and there's a 2-hour limit.
states.cars: 2 hours. No overnight parking.
states.camping: Not addressed on TDOT's page.
states.source: TDOT welcome centers and rest areas

states.name: Texas
states.answer: Yes, up to 24 hours.
states.cars: Up to 24 hours.
states.camping: Tents, shelters and other structures are prohibited.

states.name: Utah
states.answer: UDOT sets no hour limit. Extended stays are allowed and monitored. No overnight camping.
states.cars: No hour limit stated. UDOT says extended stays are permitted and monitored.
states.camping: No overnight camping.

states.name: Vermont
states.answer: Vermont sets no time limit, but overnight camping at rest areas is banned.
states.cars: No statewide time limit in the statute.
states.trucks: No separate rule in the statute.
states.camping: Overnight camping at state highway facilities, including rest areas, is prohibited unless the facility is designated for it.

states.name: Virginia
states.answer: No. Overnight parking is not permitted.
states.cars: No overnight parking at rest areas.
states.trucks: Same rule. Posted signs may add limits.
states.camping: Camping is prohibited, and so is sleeping in the rest area building.

states.name: Washington
states.answer: Yes, up to 8 hours in any 24-hour period.
states.cars: 8 hours within a 24-hour period, unless WSDOT authorizes otherwise.
states.trucks: Commercial vehicles may park up to an hour beyond federally required rest periods.
states.camping: Tents and camps are prohibited without authorization.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.answer: Not long-term. Parking over 24 hours, or a shorter posted limit, isn't allowed.
states.cars: 24 continuous hours, or the posted limit if shorter.
states.camping: Camping is prohibited.

states.name: British Columbia
states.answer: No overnight camping. Check posted hours at each rest area.
states.cars: No time limit is published. Hours vary by site on DriveBC.
states.trucks: Many rest areas fit large commercial vehicles.
states.camping: Overnight camping is not permitted.
